opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the Fourier layer isn't just a computational trick. It changes what the network is learning in the first place.

Take a standard convolutional network. You learn local filters on a fixed grid, so the model is tied to that resolution. With many scientific problems, like fluid flow, weather, or materials, the thing you actually care about is a function. The solution to a PDE lives in a continuous space, and the grid is just how you happened to sample it. So we wanted architectures that learn mappings between function spaces. That's what we call neural operators.

The Fourier operation fits that naturally. In a Fourier Neural Operator layer, you take the input function, transform it to the frequency domain, apply a learned linear transform on a truncated set of modes, and transform back. You add a pointwise linear path and a nonlinearity on top. That gives you a few things architecturally.

First, it's a global operation. A single layer sees the whole domain, unlike a convolution, which needs many layers to build up its receptive field. That matters for physics, where long-range interactions really are there.

Second, it's resolution-invariant. The parameters live on Fourier modes, not grid points, so you can train at one resolution and evaluate at another. You get zero-shot super-resolution in a principled way, because the model approximates an operator rather than memorizing a discretization.

Third, there's a good inductive bias. Many physical systems are well described by a modest number of low-frequency modes plus nonlinear interactions. Truncating modes acts as regularization, and the nonlinearities between layers let you recover higher-frequency structure. So you're not throwing information away. You're parameterizing efficiently.

I'd also stress that Fourier isn't the only choice. It's one instance of a broader idea: a kernel integral operator that you parameterize and learn. Fourier is convenient on regular domains because of the FFT. On irregular geometries you might use graph-based kernels, or learned deformations that map to a latent regular grid, or other bases like spherical harmonics on the sphere for weather and climate. The core principle is to design layers that are consistent across discretizations. Fourier just happens to be a beautifully efficient way to do that in many settings.

r001.rationale: The response describes Fourier layers as global operations in neural operators, but never says they take the place of an attention map in a transformer-like architecture.

r002.rationale: It says nonlinearities help recover higher-frequency structure, but does not connect their expressivity role to an architecture where Fourier operations replace attention.

r003.rationale: It says a single Fourier layer sees the whole domain, conveying all-to-all dependencies, and describes Fourier as an efficient approach using the FFT on regular domains.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a Fourier transform is really a change of basis, and the question is what you gain by doing your learning in that basis instead of in pixel space or grid space.

If you look at a standard convolutional network, each layer has a local receptive field. To capture long-range interactions you have to stack many layers, and even then the network is tied to the resolution it was trained on. For many of the problems I care about, like fluid flow, weather, or climate, the physics is inherently global. A disturbance in one region affects everything else, and often the right description is in terms of frequencies rather than individual grid points.

So in the Fourier neural operator, what we do is take the input function, go to Fourier space, and apply a learned linear transformation there, mode by mode. Multiplication in Fourier space is a global convolution in the original space, so in a single layer you get a receptive field covering the whole domain. Then we come back to physical space and apply a pointwise nonlinearity, because nonlinearity in Fourier space alone would not let you mix modes in a useful way. You alternate those two steps and that gives you an expressive operator.

The other thing the Fourier basis gives you is discretization invariance. The parameters live on the frequency modes, not on the grid, so you can train at one resolution and evaluate at a finer one. That is what makes it an operator in the mathematical sense, a map between function spaces, rather than just a map between fixed-size tensors. And that is the whole conceptual shift for me. Instead of thinking of a network as processing arrays, think of it as learning a solution operator for a family of PDEs.

I would also say the Fourier transform is not sacred. It is a convenient choice when the domain is periodic or roughly uniform, and we get the FFT for free, which makes everything fast. But we have done the same thing with wavelets, with spherical harmonics for global weather, and with learned transforms on irregular geometries. The architectural principle is really: pick a basis where the structure of your problem is compact, do your global mixing there, and keep your nonlinearity local in space. Fourier is just the first and cleanest instance of that idea.

r001.rationale: It describes Fourier-space global mixing but never says Fourier operations take the place of a transformer attention map.

r002.rationale: It explains that pointwise nonlinearities add expressivity, but does not describe them in an architecture where Fourier operations replace attention.

r003.rationale: It says a Fourier-space operation gives a receptive field over the whole domain in a single layer and notes that the FFT makes the approach fast, communicating global dependencies without high computational cost.

astra-6.text:
I think of Fourier operations as a way to build global interactions into the architecture. In a standard convolutional network, each layer operates on a local neighborhood, so you need multiple layers to communicate across the domain. With a Fourier transform, you move into a representation where each mode captures structure across the whole domain. You can learn how to mix and weight those modes, then transform back into physical space.

That’s the idea behind the Fourier neural operator. We combine that spectral operation with local operations and nonlinearities. The Fourier transform itself is fixed; what we learn is how to act on the representation. So it’s not just preprocessing—it’s part of the network’s computational structure.

And the broader shift is that we want to learn mappings between functions, rather than mappings between fixed-size vectors. For example, you might map an initial condition to the solution of a physical system at a later time. That gives us a way to share learned parameters across different discretizations. It doesn’t mean arbitrary fine-scale details appear for free, but it does mean the architecture isn’t intrinsically tied to one grid resolution.

r001.rationale: It describes Fourier operations as enabling global interactions, but does not say they replace a transformer’s attention map.

r002.rationale: It mentions combining Fourier operations with nonlinearities, but does not explain their role in expressivity or frame Fourier operations as replacing attention.

r003.rationale: It says Fourier modes capture structure across the whole domain, but does not state that this captures all-to-all dependencies without very high computational complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Fourier operations as a way to build global interactions into the architecture. In a standard convolutional network, each convolution operates on a local neighborhood, so you need many layers to communicate over a large distance. In Fourier space, you can transform the input, learn how to mix its frequency components, and transform it back. That gives you a global convolution.

That’s the idea behind the Fourier neural operator: we’re learning a mapping between functions, rather than just between fixed-dimensional vectors. The Fourier representation gives us an efficient way to parameterize that mapping, while nonlinearities in physical space let us represent more complex behavior. And because the parameters are associated with modes rather than individual grid points, we can share them across different resolutions. That’s particularly useful for scientific problems, where you want to learn the underlying dynamics rather than a particular discretization.

r001.rationale: The response describes Fourier operations as enabling global interactions, but does not say they replace a transformer’s attention map.

r002.rationale: It says physical-space nonlinearities represent more complex behavior, but does not connect that role to an architecture using Fourier operations in place of attention.

r003.rationale: It describes global communication and efficient parameterization, but does not state that Fourier operations capture all-to-all dependencies without very high computational complexity.
